answer_text:
As stated, the conditions do **not** determine a unique numerical limit. They only force the limit to exist and be nonnegative.

First, since

\[
-\frac{a(x)}{x}<a'(x)<0,
\]

we must have \(-a(x)/x<0\), so

\[
a(x)>0 \qquad (x>1).
\]

Thus \(a(x)\) is positive and strictly decreasing, hence bounded below by \(0\). Therefore

\[
L:=\lim_{x\to\infty}a(x)
\]

exists and satisfies \(L\ge 0\).

The differential inequality can also be written as

\[
a'(x)+\frac{a(x)}{x}>0,
\]

or equivalently,

\[
(xa(x))'=a(x)+xa'(x)>0.
\]

So \(x a(x)\) is increasing. Integrating gives only a lower bound of the form

\[
a(x)>\frac{x_0a(x_0)}{x},
\]

which tends to \(0\), but this does not force \(a(x)\to 0\).

In fact, any nonnegative limit is possible. For example, for any \(L\ge 0\), define

\[
a_L(x)=L+\frac{1}{x+1}.
\]

Then

\[
a_L'(x)=-\frac{1}{(x+1)^2}<0,
\]

and

\[
a_L'(x)+\frac{a_L(x)}{x}
=
-\frac{1}{(x+1)^2}
+\frac{L}{x}
+\frac{1}{x(x+1)}
=
\frac{L}{x}
+\frac{1}{x(x+1)^2}
>0.
\]

Hence

\[
a_L'(x)>-\frac{a_L(x)}{x},
\]

so the hypotheses are satisfied. But

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}a_L(x)=L.
\]

Therefore the given assumptions allow the limit to be \(0\), or \(1\), or any nonnegative number.

\[
\boxed{\text{The limit is not uniquely determined; it exists and can be any } L\ge 0.}
\]
